content: The study stratified hepatitis B patients based on their baseline HBV DNA levels and alanine transaminase (ALT) levels. A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted to evaluate the natural history of chronic hepatitis B (CHB) and the efficacy of antiviral therapy across different patient groups. The analysis included data from cohort studies, randomized controlled trials (RCTs), and observational studies. The outcomes assessed included the incidence of cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), and liver-related mortality. The pooled incidence rates were categorized by baseline viral load (<2000, 2000–20,000, 20,000–200,000, and ≥200,000 IU/mL) and ALT levels (normal, 1–2 times the upper limit of normal [ULN], and ≥2 times ULN). A generalized linear mixed model was used for the meta-analysis. From 13,124 identified studies, 80 were included in the analysis. The results showed that individuals with HBV DNA levels <2000 IU/mL had lower incidence rates of cirrhosis and HCC. A similar trend was observed for liver-related mortality. However, only 12 studies included children, and no clear association was found between baseline viral load and clinical outcomes in pediatric populations. The quality of evidence for treatment efficacy was very low to low for groups with lower viral loads (<2000 and 2000–20,000 IU/mL) and ranged from very low to high for higher viral load strata. Only one RCT and five observational studies reported results for patients with viral loads <2000 IU/mL or 2000–20,000 IU/mL. The findings suggest a potential interaction between higher viral loads and greater treatment efficacy for various clinical, histological, virological, and biochemical outcomes. The study highlights the urgent need for RCTs to evaluate the impact of antiviral therapy in patients with low-level viremia and early fibrosis stages, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. The lack of data on the natural history of CHB in children was identified as a research priority. The World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines for managing CHB currently recommend antiviral therapy for non-cirrhotic individuals with a baseline viral load ≥20,000 IU/mL and abnormal ALT levels. However, the efficacy of antiviral therapy in groups with lower viral loads remains uncertain. This study aimed to inform updated WHO guidelines and expand treatment criteria by providing summary estimates of treatment efficacy stratified by baseline viral load and ALT levels. The modeling of hepatitis B treatment eligibility criteria across WHO regions revealed that removing the ALT > ULN requirement had the largest impact on increasing the number of individuals eligible for treatment (75–100% increase). Lowering the viral load threshold for eligibility from ≥20,000 IU/mL to ≥2000 IU/mL increased eligibility by 37% in the African Region and 18% in the Western Pacific Region, reflecting regional differences in HBV genotype distribution. Lowering the age eligibility cut-off for treatment had a significant impact in the African Region due to the younger age structure and higher prevalence of HBV in younger cohorts. The impact of changing eligibility criteria on incidence, morbidity, and mortality was forecasted in countries like China, Ethiopia, and Pakistan. Lowering the eligibility age also reduced new HBV infections in unvaccinated cohorts, particularly in regions with low vaccination coverage. A key limitation of the study is that access to testing and treatment was not measured under each scenario. If access is provided equally across all scenarios, lowering the age cut-off is the only change forecasted to have a meaningful impact by 2030. Reducing the number of required tests is more likely to increase access to testing and treatment in regions with limited public health infrastructure. The study underscores the importance of earlier treatment for hepatitis B to reduce morbidity and mortality. However, the current model does not include data on the regression of liver disease, which has been shown to occur with treatment. Further research is needed to address these gaps and refine treatment guidelines.
